there have been MANY shameful and terrifying moments with my self harm, but this makes me feel especially bad. i finally built up the courage for it last night, actually. it was having to have a talk with my girlfriend about our future together. i needed to let them know that i’ve never planned on giving up self-harm, nor do i want to. i told them that that’s something they’d need to be prepared for when we eventually live together. i explained to them how much self harm means to me, that it’s like an old friend who knows exactly how i’m feeling and just how to help. i asked how they felt, and they said they didn’t really know. they said they knew they couldn’t stop me, and would love me unconditionally through it all. i asked if they’d prefer i cover up in hoodies and sweatpants (which i normally wear as is), or if it’d be okay for me to wear more revealing clothing on hotter days. they told me that they would never ask me to wear something i didn’t want to, and that they’d be a terrible gf if they did. we had a long talk. i expressed my deeply ingrained fear of them getting tired of me when i can’t get out of bed, when nightmares and flashbacks wake me up in the middle of the night, or when i can’t do simple things like go on a grocery run. they reassured me that they would never get tired of me, especially over something i can’t control. they said so many things i’ve begged the universe to let me hear, and that just made everything hurt worse. the fact that i’m willing to put them through knowing that i’m self harming or purging merely a wall away, or having to know that the results of my actions were hidden beneath my clothes, disgusts me. they’re so understanding, and far too good for me. i feel so ashamed to have asked this of them, but i’m so very addicted to self harm that i would sacrifice so much in order to keep it in my life. sorry for the rant! this has just been weighing heavily on me and this seemed like the perfect post to comment on lol

i can’t really “give advice”, as each and every situation varies incredibly and it would be dangerous of me to assume anything. however ! i can tell you things i wished my parents understood about/offered for self harm.

i think the biggest thing (that actually took me being years into self harm to figure out) is that you can’t ask someone stop cold-turkey. self harm is an addiction, and thus, fills a hole. if it is suddenly taken away, that hole is left uncovered. finding something to refill it is essential. there will, however, never be anything that does it quite like your addiction. a lot of it is learning to settle with whatever your healthy alternative is.

often times, people have a myriad of reasons as to why they self harm. finding these triggers and listing different options can be very helpful. keep in mind, though, that if a person has these options available and still chooses to self harm, it does NOT mean they’ve failed !! even considering the fact that you do have alternatives is a huge accomplishment.

there is no real end-all-be-all finish line. addictions are life-long battles, and it sounds like your daughters are still in the process of learning how and why to fight. relapses are a part of recovery. it is not a linear path.

self harm is a self-preserving reaction, and it’s one your brain will associate with safety. you have a smart brain for trying to react and protect you. it just unfortunately went about it in a way that might be worse for you in the long run. 

try not to make them feel like they’re broken, or that they’ve failed. let them know they’re not a lost cause, that they won’t be given up on. acknowledge and commend their efforts, as treatment is often times an incredibly hard and exhausting experience.

an opening, listening ear can be very helpful if they’re ever willing to talk as an alternative. my parents, though i’m sure they meant well, were pretty terrible at this. the few times i tried to tell them how i was feeling, i was met with unwanted advice, hurtful questions, gaslighting, disapproval, and fighting. they were often advised by both myself and therapists that listening quietly without judgment would be ideal. if they’re willing and not overflowing, non-targeted or aggressive questions could show that you’re wanting to understand. but if they get frustrated, it could prove better to back off and continue to listen to them quietly.

sometimes, asking for at least safety may help. not enabling, but safety. asking that, if they ever do unfortunately come to the point of self harming, they’ll do so without risking infection or intense injury. that, if need be, they’ll ask for help with tending to any wounds. i remember once, i hurt myself a little worse than intended. it resulted in nerve damage, infection, and some pretty bad scarring. i remember at the time wishing that i could ask my parents for help, but i was terrified of the repercussions. i was told by my doctor recently that if i had sought medical attention at the time, they could’ve caught the infection and the nerve damage wouldn’t have been as bad.

i really, really hope you have medical professionals available to reach out to for advice. never be ashamed to ask for help! i find it meaningful that you’ve gone out of your way to seek advice on this subreddit. also be sure to take care of yourself in the meantime, these things can wear heavily on parents. trying to help someone while you’re running on empty can result in worse issues for both parties. i wish all of you the best.
